name: Asisa
title: An Israelite from the Hashum clan who sent away his foreign wife
summary: Asisa was an Israelite from the Hashum clan who lived in the period after the Jewish return from exile in Babylon. He is mentioned in Ezra 10:33 among those who had married foreign women, which violated the covenant stipulations. As part of Ezra's great reform movement, Asisa committed to sending away his foreign wife. This action, however painful it was, was motivated by a desire to preserve the people's religious identity and faithfulness to the Lord at a time when the small Jewish community faced the danger of cultural and spiritual dissolution.

keyEvents.title: Listed among those who had taken foreign wives
keyEvents.description: Asisa was listed among the sons of Hashum who had married foreign women, which violated the covenant's command not to marry people from the surrounding nations.

keyEvents.title: Ezra's reform against intermarriage
keyEvents.description: Ezra led a comprehensive reform in which Israelite men who had married foreign women were required to send them away, along with their children, to restore the people's faithfulness to God's covenant.

keyEvents.title: The people's confession and pledge
keyEvents.description: The people gathered in Jerusalem, confessed their sin regarding intermarriage, and pledged to act in accordance with God's law by separating from their foreign wives.

keyEvents.title: Examination of the marriages
keyEvents.description: A commission was appointed to examine all cases of marriage to foreign women. The work was carried out systematically and completed over a period of several months.

versions.summary: Asisa was one of the sons of Shallu from the people of Israel who had taken a foreign wife during the period of return from exile. He was mentioned among those who pledged to send away their foreign wives in response to Ezra's reforms aimed at preserving the religious purity of the people.
versions.title: An Israelite who sent away his foreign wife
versions.reason: [major] Asaiah is not described as a 'leader' in the biblical text. He was an ordinary Israelite who was listed among those who had taken foreign wives. The role should be changed to something more accurate, such as 'Israelite'.; [major] According to Ezra 10:33, Asaiah is one of the sons of Mattaniah (Hebrew: Mattenai group), not Shallu. The list in Ezra 10:33 mentions "of the sons of Hashum" (or similar groupings depending on the reading). Closer examination shows that Asaiah is mentioned among the sons of Hashum in Ezra 10:33. Shallu is not mentioned as his father.; [minor] The summary mentions "the sons of Shallu" as the father, but this does not seem to agree with Ezra 10:33. Asaiah is listed among the sons of Hashum. The summary should be corrected.; [minor] There are no footnotes providing context about Ezra's reforms, the linguistic origin of the name Asaiah, or the historical background for the issue of mixed marriages in the post-exilic period.

versions.title: An Israelite who sent away his foreign wife
versions.reason: [critical] Asisa is listed among the sons of Hashum in Ezra 10:33. However, 'Hashum' is likely a clan or family name rather than a direct father. Nevertheless, this is the biblical connection given, so it can be defended to retain it. But one should note that 'the sons of Hashum' may mean descendants or members of the Hashum clan.; [minor] The summary is well written, but it could be strengthened with brief contextualization of Asisa's place within the broader list of Hashum descendants in Ezra 10:33, as well as clarifying that 'the sons of Hashum' may refer to clan affiliation.; [minor] The linguistic footnote states that the name can mean 'strength' or 'power'. The Hebrew form עֲשִׂישָׂא is rare, but a more precise connection is to the root עשׂה ('to do/act') or possibly עָשִׁישׁ ('raisin cake'). The wording should be nuanced somewhat.

footnotes.text: The name Asisa (Hebrew: עֲשִׂישָׂא) is a rare biblical name that appears only in Ezra 10:33. Its etymology is uncertain, but it may be derived from the Hebrew root עשׂה ('to do, act') or connected to עָשִׁישׁ ('raisin cake'). The rarity of the name makes it difficult to determine its exact meaning.

Ezra's reform against mixed marriages (c. 458–457 BCE) was a central but controversial measure to restore Jewish identity after the return from Babylonian exile. The practice of sending away foreign wives had roots in the prohibition against marrying Canaanite peoples found in Deuteronomy (Deut 7:1–4), where the rationale was the danger of religious apostasy.

The rabbinic tradition discusses Ezra's reform on mixed marriages in connection with questions of Jewish identity and conversion. Several rabbis in the Talmudic tradition believed that the core issue was not primarily ethnic but religious—it concerned the danger of idolatry and separation from the covenant relationship with God.

In the post-exilic period, the Jewish community was vulnerable to cultural and religious assimilation. Archaeological findings from Persian-period Judah, including pottery and seals with mixed cultural motifs, testify to a blending of cultural practices that confirms the biblical concern about religious syncretism.

The expression 'the sons of Hashum' in Ezra 10:33 likely refers to members of the Hashum clan or kinship group, not necessarily direct sons of a single individual named Hashum. Such clan designations were common in post-exilic lists and served as social and administrative categories in the rebuilt Jewish community.
